paragraphs: I've worked in and around the Lamorinda and Diablo Valley markets long enough to know when a renovation is done right, and the work at 2660 Ross Place is genuinely impressive. A full gut of electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and finishes on a 1950s West Walnut Creek home is a serious undertaking, and the result here is the kind of move-in-ready product that buyers in this price range are actively hunting for. So when I saw the listing come off market after just 28 days without a sale, it caught my attention.

Twenty-eight days is short enough that it doesn't carry the stigma of a long-stale listing, but on a fully renovated home priced at $874 per square foot, a clean exit should have happened faster. At that price point, buyers are comparing carefully, and they need more than a description that lists amenities. They need to understand exactly what distinguishes this renovation from the dozens of 'fully updated' homes they've already scrolled past. The listing had the features. It just didn't build the case for them.

I've put together a short analysis of what I think created friction in the first campaign and what a relaunch strategy would need to look like for a home like this. It's specific to 2660 Ross Place, not a generic playbook.

If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside. If you're not, I'd genuinely enjoy a conversation about what a second approach might look like. No pressure either way.

exec_summary.headline: A Fully Gut-Renovated West Walnut Creek Home  -  and a Listing That Never Built the Case for It
exec_summary.p1: 2660 Ross Place is the kind of product Walnut Creek buyers at this price point say they want: new electrical, new plumbing, new HVAC, dual pane windows, a wide-open floor plan, a gourmet kitchen with shaker cabinetry and a central island, and two primary suites on a 10,372-square-foot lot in a walkable West Walnut Creek neighborhood. This isn't a cosmetic update. It's a complete rebuild of the systems and surfaces that matter most to buyers who've been burned by deferred maintenance before.
exec_summary.p2: And yet the home came off market at 28 days without a sale. At $874 per square foot, this property sits at the upper range of the Walnut Creek premium tier, which is supportable given the scope of the renovation. But supportable on paper and felt by buyers during a search are two different things. The listing description leaned heavily on adjectives like 'opulent,' 'lavish,' and 'exquisite,' while saying almost nothing specific about what the renovation actually involved or why this home is built differently than a surface-refresh competitor. Buyers comparing carefully at this price point needed a more grounded, specific narrative, and a distribution strategy that put that narrative in front of the right audience.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to do one thing above all: translate the real scope of this renovation into buyer confidence at $874 per square foot. Every tool in the campaign should be working toward that single goal.

forensics.title: Friction #1: The Renovation Was Real  -  The Marketing Description Wasn't
forensics.body: The listing description for 2660 Ross Place read more like a luxury hotel brochure than a credible account of what this home actually is. Phrases like 'opulent bathrooms,' 'lavish,' and 'mimic a spa-like experience' are the kind of language that triggers buyer skepticism rather than buyer confidence, especially at $1,399,999 where people are reading carefully. The real story here is a complete systems overhaul on a 1956 home, new everything from panel to pipes to HVAC, and a floor plan that actually works for modern living. That story was never told. Buyers scrolling past generic luxury language never had a reason to slow down.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork listing remarks are written the way a great buyer's agent describes a home to a client, specific, credible, and built to earn trust. On Zillow Showcase, that narrative gets premium placement and is one of the first things a buyer reads, not buried in a scrolled-past description field.

forensics.title: Friction #2: $874 Per Square Foot With Nothing to Show for It Visually
forensics.body: At $874 per square foot, a buyer comparing this home against a $750-per-square-foot alternative in the same city needs to see the difference, not just read about it. A fully gut-renovated 1956 home has visual proof baked into every room: new structural systems, clean finishes, open-concept flow, spa-caliber bathrooms. But standard MLS photography captures static angles, flat lighting, and front-elevation shots that don't communicate scope. Buyers who never toured the home, which is most of them, had no way to understand what $874 per square foot actually got them here versus somewhere else.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: A 3D Matterport tour lets buyers walk every room on their own schedule, from San Francisco, from Oakland, from wherever they're searching, before they ever commit to a showing. For a renovation of this depth, that immersive walkthrough isn't a nice-to-have. It's the proof buyers need to justify the number.

forensics.title: Friction #3: A Move-In-Ready Home That the Right Buyers Never Found
forensics.body: West Walnut Creek at $1.4 million is not a casual local search. The buyers most likely to pay a premium for a fully renovated, no-deferred-maintenance home in this neighborhood are professionals relocating from San Francisco or Oakland, buyers who've been renting while rates were high and are now ready to move decisively into something they don't have to touch. Those buyers were not browsing the Walnut Creek MLS waiting for this listing to appear. They needed to be reached where they were actively researching Lamorinda and Diablo Valley before they'd found a specific address. A passive MLS presence doesn't do that.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork runs geo-targeted digital campaigns aimed at SF and East Bay buyers who are researching this corridor but haven't yet committed to a neighborhood, putting this home in front of decision-ready buyers before they've found a competing listing.

positioning_table.verdict: At $874/sqft versus a benchmark range of $820-$950/sqft, this home sits in the middle of that range. At $874 per square foot, 2660 Ross Place sits near the middle of Walnut Creek's premium renovation tier, and the scope of work here genuinely supports that positioning. The gap isn't in the numbers. It's that the marketing never gave buyers the specific, credible evidence they needed to feel confident meeting the price. A relaunch built around visual proof and a grounded renovation narrative would put this home in a much stronger position.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Tell the Renovation Story in Buyer Language
pillars.body: New electrical panel, new plumbing, new HVAC, new windows, new flooring, new kitchen, new bathrooms. That's not a cosmetic refresh. That's a home rebuilt from the inside out, and buyers at $1.4 million need to feel the weight of that before they schedule a showing. The relaunch campaign starts with a complete rewrite of the listing narrative, specific, grounded, and credible, paired with a Zillow Showcase placement that puts that story front and center on the platform where most buyers begin.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Give Buyers Visual Proof That Earns the Price
pillars.body: At $874 per square foot, buyers are doing a mental comparison against every other option in their search. The two primary suites, the open-concept kitchen and living flow, the quality of the bathroom finishes, and the scale of the lot all need to be experienced visually before a buyer will drive to Walnut Creek for a showing. A full Matterport 3D walkthrough gives out-of-area and time-constrained buyers the ability to tour this home on their own terms, from anywhere, at any hour, and arrive at the showing already emotionally invested rather than still evaluating.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Find the Buyers Who Are Ready for Exactly This Home
pillars.body: The buyer most likely to pay a premium for a turnkey, no-surprises renovation in West Walnut Creek is probably not searching the local MLS right now. They are researching the Lamorinda and Diablo Valley corridor from San Francisco or Oakland, comparing neighborhoods, and waiting for something that removes the renovation risk they've seen in everything else. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put 2660 Ross Place directly in front of that audience while they are still in research mode, before they've settled on a competing neighborhood or a competing listing.
